etymology: From the Greek ampelos, “vine,” with alēthinos, “true” or “genuine,” the last of the great I AM sayings of the Gospel of John.
biblical_def: In the night of His betrayal the Lord Jesus said unto His disciples, I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman (Joh 15:1). He set Himself forth under the figure of the vine and His people as the branches, that they might know there is no life, no fruit, no standing in them save as they abide in Him. Every branch in Him that beareth not fruit the Father taketh away, and every fruitful branch He purgeth, that it may bring forth more fruit (Joh 15:2). And the Lord pressed the great word of dependence: Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself, except it abide in the vine; no more can ye, except ye abide in me (Joh 15:4). He that abideth in Him bringeth forth much fruit; for without Me, He said, ye can do nothing (Joh 15:5). The dictionary marks the true vine as the figure of the believer’s living union with Christ, from whom alone all grace and fruitfulness flow. So the Scripture teaches that fruit is not the root of life but the proof of it, and that the branches which abide are kept by the husbandman’s own care unto perseverance and increase. The barren branch, cast forth and withered and burned (Joh 15:6), was never truly joined; but they that abide bear much fruit, and herein, the Lord saith, is the Father glorified.
webster_summary: The figure under which Christ sets forth Himself as the source of all life and fruit, and His people as branches that must abide in Him.
webster_full: THE TRUE VINE, the last of the I AM sayings, spoken on the night of the betrayal.
Christ is the vine and the Father the husbandman, who purgeth the fruitful branches.
The branches must abide in the vine, or they can bear no fruit at all.
Without Christ the believer can do nothing; abiding in Him he beareth much fruit.
The barren branch is cast forth and burned, never having been truly joined.
scriptures: Joh 15:1
I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman.
Joh 15:4
Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself, except it abide in the vine; no more can ye, except ye abide in me.
Joh 15:5
I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing.
Joh 15:8
Herein is my Father glorified, that ye bear much fruit; so shall ye be my disciples.
corruption_summary: A saying of Christ that has drawn little redefinition; it teaches the believer’s living union with Christ and the perseverance of the fruitful branch.
corruption_paragraphs: The figure of the true vine has drawn little redefinition from the present age, surviving as one of the best-loved of the Lord’s sayings. The dictionary records it that the reader may mark the doctrine of union with Christ and the fruit-bearing it works in His own.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the believer’s living union with Christ, from whom alone all fruit flows. Without Him we can do nothing; the branch hath no life of itself, but only as it abides in the vine. So the Scripture cuts off all boasting in works as the root of salvation, and yet calls the saint to bring forth much fruit, which is the appointed proof of true abiding. The fruitful branch is purged by the husbandman that it may bear more, and is kept unto perseverance by the same hand that joined it; for they that are truly in Christ abide, and they that abide bear much fruit, to the glory of the Father.
roots_summary: From the Greek for “true vine,” the saying names the union of Christ and His people as vine and branches.
roots_lines: The True Vine — Greek ampelos alēthinē, the figure of Christ and His branches.
It is the last of the great I AM sayings in the Gospel of John.
The Father is the husbandman, who purgeth the fruitful branches.
The branches can bear no fruit except they abide in the vine.
Without Christ the believer can do nothing, but abiding beareth much fruit.
usage: Like the branch in the true vine, the believer beareth fruit only as he abides in Christ.
Without me ye can do nothing; abide in me, and ye shall bring forth much fruit.
The husbandman purgeth the fruitful branch, that it may bring forth more fruit.

etymology: From the Greek artos tēs zōēs, “bread of life,” the great I AM saying spoken after the feeding of the five thousand.
biblical_def: After He had fed the five thousand, and the multitude sought Him again for the loaves, the Lord Jesus turned their hunger to the true food, and said, I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger; and he that believeth on me shall never thirst (Joh 6:35). He set Himself forth as the bread which came down from heaven, of which if a man eat he shall live for ever; and that bread, He said, is My flesh, which I will give for the life of the world (Joh 6:51). The eating of which He spake is the believing reception of Christ crucified, by which the soul is nourished unto everlasting life. And in this discourse the Lord laid bare the sovereign ground of all coming to Him: No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him (Joh 6:44); and again, All that the Father giveth me shall come to me; and him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out (Joh 6:37). The dictionary marks the bread of life as the figure of Christ given for and received by His people. So the Scripture teaches the effectual drawing of the Father, that none come of their own unaided will, but only those whom the Father giveth and draweth; and these all come, and are received, and raised up at the last day, for the Lord loseth none the Father hath given Him.
webster_summary: The figure under which Christ sets Himself forth as the heavenly food received by faith unto eternal life.
webster_full: THE BREAD OF LIFE, the I AM saying spoken after the feeding of the five thousand.
He that cometh to Christ shall never hunger, and he that believeth shall never thirst.
The bread is His flesh, given for the life of the world and received by faith.
No man can come to Christ except the Father draw him.
All that the Father giveth Him shall come, and He will in no wise cast them out.
scriptures: Joh 6:35
And Jesus said unto them, I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger; and he that believeth on me shall never thirst.
Joh 6:37

Joh 6:44

corruption_summary: A saying of Christ that has drawn little redefinition; it teaches Christ as the soul’s food and the Father’s effectual drawing of His own.
corruption_paragraphs: The bread of life has drawn little redefinition from the present age, surviving as one of the great I AM sayings of the Gospel of John. The dictionary records it that the reader may mark both the figure of Christ as the soul’s food and the sovereign drawing of the Father woven through the discourse.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the effectual drawing of the Father, that no man comes to Christ of his own unaided will. No man can come except the Father draw him; and all that the Father giveth come, and are received, and are raised up at the last day. So the Scripture lays the whole work of salvation in the hand of God, who gives a people to His Son and draws them home; and the believer feeds on Christ, the bread which came down from heaven, and shall never hunger nor be cast out, for the Lord loseth none of all that the Father hath given Him.
roots_summary: From the Greek for “bread of life,” the saying names Christ as the heavenly food received by faith.
roots_lines: The Bread of Life — Greek artos tēs zōēs, the heavenly food.
It is the I AM saying spoken after the feeding of the five thousand.
Christ is the living bread come down from heaven, given for the life of the world.
No man can come to Him except the Father draw him.
All that the Father giveth come, and He will in no wise cast them out.
usage: Like the manna in the wilderness, the bread of life is Christ given for His people.
He that cometh to me shall never hunger; and he that believeth on me shall never thirst.
No man can come to Christ except the Father which hath sent Him draw him.

etymology: From the Greek to phōs tou kosmou, “the light of the world,” an I AM saying spoken by Christ in the temple.
biblical_def: As He taught in the treasury of the temple, the Lord Jesus lifted up the great word, I am the light of the world: he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life (Joh 8:12). The world lay in the darkness of sin and ignorance and death, and into that darkness Christ came as the true Light, which lighteth every man that cometh into the world (Joh 1:9). He spake again the same word before He gave sight to the man born blind: As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world (Joh 9:5), and then opened the blind eyes for a sign that He came to give light to them that sat in darkness. The dictionary marks the light of the world as the figure of Christ dispelling the darkness of sin by His person and His truth, and giving the light of life to all that follow Him. So the Scripture teaches that men love darkness rather than light, because their deeds are evil (Joh 3:19), and cannot come to the light of themselves; but they whom He calls He draws out of darkness into His marvellous light, and they walk no more in the night. To follow Christ is to have the light of life, for there is no other light that scatters the darkness of a fallen world, and they that walk by Him stumble not, but are led safely home.
webster_summary: The figure under which Christ sets Himself forth as the true Light that dispels the darkness of sin and gives light of life to His followers.
webster_full: THE LIGHT OF THE WORLD, the I AM saying spoken by Christ in the temple.
He that followeth Christ shall not walk in darkness, but have the light of life.
The world lay in darkness, and Christ came as the true Light into it.
He spake the same word before He gave sight to the man born blind.
Men love darkness rather than light, because their deeds are evil.
scriptures: Joh 8:12
Then spake Jesus again unto them, saying, I am the light of the world: he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life.
Joh 9:5
As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world.

That was the true Light, which lighteth every man that cometh into the world.
Joh 3:19

corruption_summary: A saying of Christ that has drawn little redefinition; it teaches Christ as the true Light that scatters the darkness of sin.
corruption_paragraphs: The light of the world has drawn little redefinition from the present age, surviving as one of the most cherished of the I AM sayings. The dictionary records it that the reader may mark the figure of Christ as the true Light dispelling the darkness of a fallen world.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Christ alone is the Light that scatters the darkness of sin and death. The world lay in darkness, and men loved that darkness because their deeds were evil; they could not come to the light of themselves. But Christ is the true Light, and they whom He calls He draws out of darkness into His marvellous light. To follow Him is to have the light of life, and to walk no more in the night; for there is no other light that can lighten a fallen world, and they that walk by Him are led safely home.
roots_summary: From the Greek for “the light of the world,” the saying names Christ as the true Light of men.
roots_lines: The Light of the World — Greek to phōs tou kosmou, the true Light.
It is an I AM saying spoken by Christ in the temple.
He that followeth Him shall not walk in darkness, but have the light of life.
He spake it again before He gave sight to the man born blind.
The world lay in darkness until the true Light came into it.
usage: Like the dawn upon a long night, Christ the light of the world scatters the darkness of sin.
He that followeth me shall not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life.
Men loved darkness rather than light, because their deeds were evil.

etymology: From the Greek thura, “door” or “gate,” the I AM saying by which Christ declares Himself the one entrance into salvation.
biblical_def: In the discourse of the shepherd and the sheepfold, the Lord Jesus said plainly, I am the door of the sheep (Joh 10:7), and again, I am the door: by me if any man enter in, he shall be saved, and shall go in and out, and find pasture (Joh 10:9). He set Himself forth as the one and only entrance into the fold of God, that as the sheep pass into safety and pasture through the door, so men are saved only through Him. All that ever came before Him, the false shepherds and thieves, were robbers; but the sheep did not hear them (Joh 10:8). The dictionary marks the door of the sheep as the figure of Christ the sole way of salvation, by whom alone a man enters into life. So the Scripture teaches that there is none other name under heaven given among men whereby we must be saved (Act 4:12), and shuts up every other gate. He that climbeth up some other way, by works, by birth, by religion of his own making, is a thief and a robber and never enters the fold; but he that enters by the Door is saved, and finds safety within and pasture without, kept by the Good Shepherd who is Himself the gate. There is one door, and Christ is that door, and no man cometh unto the Father but by Him.
webster_summary: The figure under which Christ declares Himself the one and only entrance into salvation and the fold of God.
webster_full: THE DOOR OF THE SHEEP, the I AM saying of Christ in the shepherd discourse.
By Him if any man enter in, he shall be saved, and find pasture.
He is the one and only entrance into the fold of God.
All that came before Him as false shepherds were thieves and robbers.
He that climbeth up some other way never truly enters the fold.
scriptures: Joh 10:7
Then said Jesus unto them again, Verily, verily, I say unto you, I am the door of the sheep.
Joh 10:9
I am the door: by me if any man enter in, he shall be saved, and shall go in and out, and find pasture.
Joh 10:1
Verily, verily, I say unto you, He that entereth not by the door into the sheepfold, but climbeth up some other way, the same is a thief and a robber.
Act 4:12
Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved.
corruption_summary: A saying of Christ that has drawn little redefinition; it teaches Christ as the sole door of salvation, shutting up every other way.
corruption_paragraphs: The door of the sheep has drawn little redefinition from the present age, surviving as one of the plainest of the I AM sayings. The dictionary records it that the reader may mark the figure of Christ as the one and only entrance into the fold of God.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Christ is the sole door of salvation, and there is no other way into the fold. By Him if any man enter in, he shall be saved; but he that climbeth up some other way, by works or birth or self-made religion, is a thief and a robber and never enters. So the Scripture shuts up every other gate, for there is none other name under heaven given among men whereby we must be saved. There is one door, and Christ is that door; and they that enter by Him find safety within and pasture without, kept by the Shepherd who is Himself the gate.
roots_summary: From the Greek for “door,” the saying names Christ as the one entrance into salvation.
roots_lines: The Door of the Sheep — Greek thura, “door” or “gate.”
It is an I AM saying in the shepherd discourse of John 10.
By Christ if any man enter in, he shall be saved and find pasture.
He is the one and only entrance into the fold of God.
He that climbeth up some other way is a thief and a robber.
usage: Like the gate of a fold, Christ the door admits His sheep into safety and pasture.
I am the door: by me if any man enter in, he shall be saved.
There is none other name under heaven whereby we must be saved.

etymology: From the Greek ho poimēn ho kalos, “the good shepherd,” the I AM saying in which Christ declares He layeth down His life for the sheep.
biblical_def: In the tenth chapter of John the Lord Jesus said, I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep (Joh 10:11), and twice over, I lay down my life for the sheep (Joh 10:15). He set Himself forth as the Shepherd who knows His own and is known of them, even as the Father knoweth Him and He the Father; and His knowing and His dying are particular: not for sheep in general, but for the sheep, His sheep, given Him of the Father. He marked the difference between His own and the rest: ye believe not, because ye are not of my sheep. My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me (Joh 10:26, 27). To these He gives eternal life, and they shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of His hand (Joh 10:28). The dictionary marks the good shepherd discourse as the great Johannine witness to particular, definite redemption: Christ laid down His life not in a vague intention toward all, but effectually for the sheep the Father gave Him, every one of whom He calls by name, keeps to the end, and raises up at the last day. So the Scripture teaches that the cross was no failed offer but a finished and effectual work, by which the Shepherd purchased His flock, knows each of them, and brings them safely home, that not one of them is lost.
webster_summary: The I AM discourse in which Christ declares He layeth down His life for the sheep, teaching particular and definite redemption.
webster_full: THE GOOD SHEPHERD DISCOURSE, the I AM saying of John 10.
The good shepherd giveth, and layeth down, His life for the sheep.
He knows His own and is known of them, as the Father knoweth Him.
His sheep hear His voice, and He gives them eternal life.
None shall pluck them out of His hand, for He keeps them to the end.
scriptures: I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep.
As the Father knoweth me, even so know I the Father: and I lay down my life for the sheep.
My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me:
And I give unto them eternal life; and they shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand.
corruption_summary: A saying of Christ corrupted by the universal-atonement reading; it teaches that Christ laid down His life effectually for His own sheep, not for all in general.
corruption_paragraphs: The good shepherd discourse is pressed by some into a universalist or general-atonement mould, as though Christ laid down His life equally for every man without distinction, so that the cross secured nothing in particular and only made salvation possible for all alike. But this is to read past the very words the Shepherd spake; for He says not that He died for the world without distinction, but I lay down my life for the sheep, and again, ye believe not, because ye are not of my sheep.

The Scripture answers the universalist reading on its own ground. Christ’s dying is particular and effectual: He giveth His life for the sheep, He knoweth them, He calleth them, and to them, and not to the goats, He giveth eternal life with the promise that they shall never perish. Were the atonement for all without distinction, then either all must be saved (which Scripture denies) or Christ’s blood failed for the many who perish (which dishonours His finished work). The Reformed and confessional doctrine of definite redemption is the plain sense of the discourse: the Shepherd purchased His flock, knows each by name, and loseth none. This is no narrowing of grace but the strength of it, for a redemption that actually saves is greater than a redemption that only might.
roots_summary: From the Greek for “the good shepherd,” the saying names Christ as He who layeth down His life for His own sheep.
roots_lines: The Good Shepherd Discourse — Greek ho poimēn ho kalos, the good shepherd.
It is the I AM saying of the tenth chapter of John.
The good shepherd layeth down His life for the sheep.
He knoweth His own and is known of them, and they hear His voice.
He giveth them eternal life, and none shall pluck them from His hand.
usage: Like a shepherd who dies to save his flock, Christ laid down His life for the sheep.
My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.
None shall pluck them out of His hand, for the Shepherd keeps His own.

etymology: From the Greek hydōr zōn, “living water,” the figure under which Christ offers the Spirit to them that believe.
biblical_def: At the well of Samaria the Lord Jesus offered the woman a gift greater than the water of Jacob’s well: Whosoever drinketh of this water shall thirst again: but whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst; but the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life (Joh 4:14). And in the last day, that great day of the feast, He stood and cried, saying, If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink (Joh 7:37); and the Scripture itself interprets the figure: But this spake he of the Spirit, which they that believe on him should receive (Joh 7:39). The living water, then, is the Holy Ghost, given by Christ to dwell within His people and to spring up unto everlasting life. The dictionary marks the water of life as the figure of the Spirit poured out upon believers, satisfying the thirsty soul as no earthly thing can. So the Scripture teaches that the gift is free, offered to whosoever thirsts, and yet is given only to them that come and believe; and that the Spirit, once given, is no passing draught but an inward and abiding fountain, a well of water springing up within, by which the soul is forever quickened and the believer never thirsts again with the parching thirst of sin. They that drink of this water are satisfied unto everlasting life.
webster_summary: The figure of the living water, by which Christ promises the Holy Ghost as an abiding fountain to all that believe.
webster_full: THE WATER OF LIFE, the figure of the living water offered by Christ.
He offered it to the woman of Samaria at Jacob’s well.
Whosoever drinketh of it shall never thirst, but have a well springing up to life.
At the feast He cried, If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink.
The Scripture interprets the living water as the Spirit whom believers receive.
scriptures: Joh 4:14
But whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst; but the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life.
Joh 7:37
In the last day, that great day of the feast, Jesus stood and cried, saying, If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink.
Joh 7:38
He that believeth on me, as the scripture hath said, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water.
Joh 7:39
(But this spake he of the Spirit, which they that believe on him should receive: for the Holy Ghost was not yet given; because that Jesus was not yet glorified.)
corruption_summary: A saying of Christ that has drawn little redefinition; it teaches the gift of the Spirit as an abiding fountain to believers.
corruption_paragraphs: The water of life has drawn little redefinition from the present age, surviving as a beloved figure of the Gospel of John. The dictionary records it that the reader may mark the gift of the Holy Ghost which the Lord offers to the thirsty soul.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the gift of the Spirit, freely offered to whosoever thirsts and given to them that come and believe. The living water, the Scripture itself declares, is the Spirit whom they that believe should receive; and He is no passing draught but an abiding fountain, a well of water springing up within unto everlasting life. So the dictionary honours the free and earnest offer of Christ, If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink, while teaching that the drinking is the coming of faith, and the water the indwelling Spirit, by whom the believer is quickened and satisfied and shall never thirst again with the thirst of sin.
roots_summary: From the Greek for “living water,” the figure names the Spirit given by Christ to them that believe.
roots_lines: The Water of Life — Greek hydōr zōn, “living water.”
Christ offered it to the woman of Samaria at the well.
Whosoever drinketh of it shall never thirst again.
It is a well of water springing up into everlasting life.
The Scripture interprets the living water as the Spirit believers receive.
usage: Like a fountain in a dry land, the water of life is the Spirit Christ gives His own.
If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink.
The water Christ gives is a well springing up into everlasting life.

etymology: From the Greek gennathenai anōthen, “to be born again” or “born from above,” the necessity Christ declared to Nicodemus.
biblical_def: When Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews, came to Jesus by night, the Lord met all his learning with a word he could not master: Verily, verily, I say unto thee, Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God (Joh 3:3). And when Nicodemus marvelled, asking how a man could be born when he is old, the Lord pressed the necessity: Except a man be born of water and of the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God (Joh 3:5). That which is born of the flesh is flesh; and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit (Joh 3:6); the natural man, dead in sin, can neither beget nor quicken himself, but must be born anew from above by the sovereign work of the Holy Ghost. And the Lord likened the Spirit’s working to the wind: The wind bloweth where it listeth, and thou hearest the sound thereof, but canst not tell whence it cometh, and whither it goeth: so is every one that is born of the Spirit (Joh 3:8). The dictionary marks the new birth as regeneration, the monergistic and sovereign act of the Spirit by which a dead soul is made alive. So the Scripture teaches that regeneration is wholly God’s work, not man’s decision nor man’s preparing; the Spirit quickeneth whom He will. Man cannot born himself again any more than a child begets itself; the new birth is from above, of God.
webster_summary: The sovereign and monergistic work of the Spirit by which a dead soul is born again from above, declared by Christ to Nicodemus.
webster_full: THE NEW BIRTH, the necessity Christ declared to Nicodemus by night.
Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.
That which is born of the flesh is flesh, and of the Spirit is spirit.
The natural man cannot quicken himself, but must be born from above.
The wind bloweth where it listeth: so is every one that is born of the Spirit.
scriptures: Joh 3:3

Joh 3:5
Jesus answered, Verily, verily, I say unto thee, Except a man be born of water and of the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God.
Joh 3:6
That which is born of the flesh is flesh; and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit.
Joh 3:8
The wind bloweth where it listeth, and thou hearest the sound thereof, but canst not tell whence it cometh, and whither it goeth: so is every one that is born of the Spirit.
corruption_summary: The new birth is corrupted when “born again” is reduced to a decisional or merely emotional experience; the Scripture teaches a sovereign, monergistic regeneration.
corruption_paragraphs: The phrase “born again” has in the present age been hollowed of its meaning. Among much modern revivalism it is reduced to a decisional or merely emotional experience, a sinner’s prayer prayed, a moment of feeling, a card signed, an aisle walked, as though the new birth were a thing a man works in himself by an act of his own will. This is to make regeneration the fruit of man’s decision rather than the cause of his faith, and to turn the sovereign quickening of the Spirit into a transaction the natural man performs.

The Lord’s own words to Nicodemus rebut this reduction. The new birth is from above, by water and the Spirit, and that which is born of the flesh is only flesh; the dead soul can no more born itself again than a child can beget itself. The wind bloweth where it listeth, and so is every one that is born of the Spirit, which is to say the Spirit quickeneth whom He will, sovereignly and effectually, and the believing follows. The dictionary recovers the Reformed and confessional doctrine: regeneration is monergistic, the act of God alone, prior to and the cause of faith and repentance. It is not the sinner’s achievement nor a passing emotion, but the sovereign work of the Holy Ghost, raising the dead to life.
roots_summary: From the Greek for “born from above,” the new birth names the Spirit’s sovereign work of regeneration.
roots_lines: The New Birth — Greek gennathenai anōthen, “born again” or “born from above.”
Christ declared it to Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews, by night.
Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.
It is the sovereign, monergistic work of the Holy Ghost.
The wind bloweth where it listeth: so is every one born of the Spirit.
usage: Like a dead man raised, the soul born again is quickened by the sovereign Spirit.
Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.
The wind bloweth where it listeth: so is every one that is born of the Spirit.

word: The Washing of the Disciples’ Feet
etymology: From the Greek niptein tous podas, “to wash the feet,” the act of Christ before the last Passover supper in the Gospel of John.
biblical_def: Before the feast of the passover, knowing that His hour was come, and having loved His own which were in the world, He loved them unto the end (Joh 13:1). And the Lord Jesus rose from supper, laid aside His garments, and took a towel and girded Himself; then He poured water into a bason, and began to wash the disciples’ feet, and to wipe them with the towel wherewith He was girded (Joh 13:4, 5). The Master of all stooped to the office of the lowest servant, and washed even the feet of Judas who should betray Him. When Peter, ashamed, would have forbidden it, the Lord said, If I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me (Joh 13:8), teaching that without His cleansing there is no fellowship with Him. And when He had washed their feet and taken His garments again, He set the deed before them as a pattern: If I then, your Lord and Master, have washed your feet; ye also ought to wash one another's feet (Joh 13:14). The dictionary marks the washing of the disciples’ feet as the great act of Christ’s humility and the model of His servant-love. So the Scripture teaches that He who was Lord of all took upon Him the form of a servant; and that His people, having been washed by Him, are bound to lowly love and mutual service, esteeming others better than themselves, for the servant is not greater than his lord.
webster_summary: The act in which Christ, the Lord and Master, washed His disciples’ feet as a pattern of humility and servant-love.
webster_full: THE WASHING OF THE DISCIPLES’ FEET, the act of Christ before the last supper.
Having loved His own, He loved them unto the end.
He laid aside His garments, girded Himself, and washed their feet.
If I wash thee not, He said to Peter, thou hast no part with me.
Ye also ought, He said, to wash one another's feet.
scriptures: Joh 13:1

Now before the feast of the passover, when Jesus knew that his hour was come that he should depart out of this world unto the Father, having loved his own which were in the world, he loved them unto the end.
Joh 13:5
After that he poureth water into a bason, and began to wash the disciples’ feet, and to wipe them with the towel wherewith he was girded.
Joh 13:8
Peter saith unto him, Thou shalt never wash my feet. Jesus answered him, If I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me.
If I then, your Lord and Master, have washed your feet; ye also ought to wash one another's feet.
corruption_summary: An act of Christ that has drawn little redefinition; it teaches His humility and the believer’s call to lowly, mutual service.
corruption_paragraphs: The washing of the disciples’ feet has drawn little redefinition from the present age, surviving as one of the most moving scenes in the Gospel of John. The dictionary records it that the reader may mark both Christ’s deep humility and the example He left to His own.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the humility and servant-love of Christ, and the lowly love it binds upon His people. He who was Lord and Master stooped to the office of the lowest servant, washing even the feet of His betrayer, and said, If I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me, that without His cleansing there is no fellowship with Him. Then He made the deed a pattern: ye also ought to wash one another's feet. So the saint, having himself been washed by Christ, is taught to esteem others better than himself and to serve them in love, for the servant is not greater than his lord, nor he that is sent greater than he that sent him.
roots_summary: From the Greek for “to wash the feet,” the act names Christ’s humility and the pattern of servant-love.
roots_lines: The Washing of the Feet — Greek niptein tous podas, “to wash the feet.”

He set it as a pattern: ye also ought to wash one another's feet.
usage: Like a servant girding himself with a towel, Christ washed the feet of His own.
If I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me.
Ye also ought to wash one another's feet, for the servant is not greater than his lord.

etymology: From the Greek proseuchē, “prayer,” so called because in it Christ intercedes for His own as the great High Priest in the seventeenth chapter of John.
biblical_def: On the night before His passion, having finished His discourse, the Lord Jesus lifted up His eyes to heaven and prayed to His Father for Himself, for His apostles, and for all that should believe through their word (Joh 17). It is rightly called the high priestly prayer, for in it the great High Priest intercedes for His people before He goes to offer Himself for them. And the prayer is particular, not general: I pray for them, He saith; I pray not for the world, but for them which thou hast given me; for they are thine (Joh 17:9). He prayed that the Father would keep them, sanctify them through the truth, and make them one; and He stretched the prayer beyond the eleven: Neither pray I for these alone, but for them also which shall believe on me through their word (Joh 17:20). The dictionary marks the high priestly prayer as the great pattern and proof of Christ’s particular intercession for His own. So the Scripture teaches that Christ ever liveth to make intercession, and that His intercession is for a definite people, the same the Father gave Him and for whom He died, and not for the world as such. As He prayed in that hour for them and not for the world, so He pleads now for the elect; and because His intercession is particular and prevailing, they whom He prays for are kept, sanctified, and brought at last to behold His glory.
webster_summary: The prayer of John 17 in which Christ, as great High Priest, intercedes particularly for His own and not for the world.
webster_full: THE HIGH PRIESTLY PRAYER, the prayer of Christ in the seventeenth chapter of John.
He prayed it on the night before His passion, lifting His eyes to heaven.
I pray not for the world, He said, but for them which thou hast given me.
He prayed also for all that should believe through the apostles’ word.
It is the great pattern of His particular and prevailing intercession.
scriptures: Joh 17:9
I pray for them: I pray not for the world, but for them which thou hast given me; for they are thine.
Neither pray I for these alone, but for them also which shall believe on me through their word;
Father, I will that they also, whom thou hast given me, be with me where I am; that they may behold my glory, which thou hast given me: for thou lovedst me before the foundation of the world.
Heb 7:25
Wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him, seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them.
corruption_summary: A prayer of Christ that has drawn little redefinition; it teaches His particular intercession for the people the Father gave Him.
corruption_paragraphs: The high priestly prayer has drawn little redefinition from the present age, surviving as one of the most solemn passages of the Gospel of John. The dictionary records it that the reader may mark the particular and prevailing intercession of Christ for His own.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the particular intercession of Christ for the people the Father gave Him. In that hour He said plainly, I pray not for the world, but for them which thou hast given me; His prayer was for a definite people, the same for whom He was about to die. So the Scripture teaches that Christ ever liveth to make intercession, and that His pleading at the Father’s right hand is for the elect, the very ones He redeemed. Because His intercession is particular and prevailing, they whom He prays for are kept, sanctified through the truth, made one, and brought at last to behold His glory; for the Son’s prayer is never refused of the Father.
roots_summary: From the prayer of John 17, the name marks Christ’s priestly intercession for His own.

usage: Like a priest pleading for his people, Christ in John 17 interceded for His own.

etymology: From the Greek kokkos tou sitou, “grain” or “corn of wheat,” the figure by which Christ foretold His fruitful death.
biblical_def: When certain Greeks came up to worship at the feast and desired to see Jesus, the Lord knew that the hour was come that the Son of man should be glorified, and He answered with a figure drawn from the field: Verily, verily, I say unto you, Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit (Joh 12:24). He spake of His own death, that He must be put into the ground like a buried seed, and out of that death should spring a harvest of redeemed souls. As the single grain perishes that many may grow, so Christ must die that He might not abide alone, but gather a great multitude into life. And He drew the law of discipleship from the same figure: He that loveth his life shall lose it; and he that hateth his life in this world shall keep it unto life eternal (Joh 12:25). The dictionary marks the grain of wheat as the figure of Christ’s death bearing much fruit. So the Scripture teaches that the cross was no defeat but the very seed of the harvest, the appointed way by which the Son of man, lifted up, should draw all His own unto Himself. His dying was fruitful dying, the planting of the one grain from which springs the whole church of the redeemed; and they that follow Him are taught the same law of the life laid down.
webster_summary: The figure by which Christ foretold that His death, like a buried seed, would bring forth a great harvest of redeemed souls.

But if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit, as Christ’s death bears a harvest.
He that hateth his life in this world shall keep it unto life eternal.

corruption_summary: A saying of Christ that has drawn little redefinition; it teaches that His death, like a buried seed, brings forth much fruit.
corruption_paragraphs: The grain of wheat has drawn little redefinition from the present age, surviving as a tender figure of the Lord’s fruitful death. The dictionary records it that the reader may mark how the cross is set forth not as defeat but as the seed of a great harvest.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Christ’s death was fruitful death, the planting of the one grain from which springs the whole church of the redeemed. Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone; but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit. So the Lord must be buried like a seed that He might not abide alone, but gather a great multitude into life. The cross was no failure but the appointed way of the harvest; and the same figure teaches the disciple that he who hateth his life in this world keepeth it unto life eternal, for the life laid down for Christ’s sake is the life that bears fruit unto God.
